modules.name: Autism Information Module
modules.description: The essentials — what ASD is, how it shows up differently in every child, and what the research says about early signs.

articles.title: What is Autism Spectrum Disorder?
articles.html:
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that shapes how a person communicates, interacts socially, and experiences the world around them. "Spectrum" is the key word — no two autistic children look or behave the same way, and support needs can range widely from one child to the next.

Rather than a checklist of deficits, think of ASD as a different way of processing and relating to the world — one shaped by each child's unique wiring, environment, and relationships. Researchers increasingly describe autism as a phenomenon best understood in context: in the home, with family, and across daily routines, not just inside a clinic room.

What this means for you as a parent: your day-to-day observations at home are genuinely valuable information, not just anecdotes. You know your child's patterns better than a single assessment ever could.

articles.title: Every Child is Different
articles.html:
Because ASD affects each child differently, the same strategy that works beautifully for one family may need real adjusting for yours. That's normal, not a sign you're doing something wrong.

  • Some children are highly verbal; others communicate mainly through gesture, behavior, or assistive tools.
  • Sensory needs vary — a sound that soothes one child may overwhelm another.
  • Routines, interests, and comfort levels are deeply individual.

The goal of this app isn't to hand you a single formula. It's to give you a range of evidence-informed options you can adapt to your own child, your own home, and your own family's rhythm.

articles.title: Early Signs to Notice
articles.html:
Early signs can include differences in eye contact, delayed or unusual language development, strong preferences for routine, intense focus on specific interests, and distinct responses to sound, texture, or light.

None of these signs on their own means a diagnosis — children develop at their own pace. But if a pattern feels persistent and you're noticing it across different settings (home, school, with relatives), it's worth raising with a developmental pediatrician.

This is general information, not a diagnostic tool. Only a licensed developmental pediatrician or psychologist can assess and diagnose ASD.

modules.name: Communication and Sensory Support System
modules.description: Bridging verbal and non-verbal communication, and understanding sensory sensitivities day to day.

articles.title: Visual Supports That Help
articles.html:
Many autistic children process visual information more easily than spoken words alone. Pairing speech with pictures, gestures, or simple signs can make daily instructions land more clearly.

  • Visual schedules — a simple picture sequence of the day's routine reduces anxiety around "what's next."
  • First-then boards — "first brush teeth, then tablet time" gives a concrete, visible structure.
  • Gesture + word pairing — pointing while naming an object reinforces meaning for both verbal and non-verbal learners.

Consistency matters more than complexity — the same handful of visual cues, used daily, tend to work better than an elaborate system used occasionally.

articles.title: Understanding Sensory Sensitivities
articles.html:
Many children with ASD experience sound, light, touch, taste, or movement more intensely — or less intensely — than typical. A tag on clothing, fluorescent lighting, or a crowded room can be genuinely distressing, not "misbehavior."

Small home adjustments can go a long way: noise-reducing headphones for loud events, soft or seamless clothing, a quiet corner to retreat to, and warning your child before a sensory-heavy transition (like leaving a noisy mall).

Watching for your child's individual sensory patterns — what calms them, what overwhelms them — is one of the most powerful tools a parent has.

articles.title: Building Two-Way Communication
articles.html:
Communication isn't only about your child understanding you — it's also about you learning to read their cues, even non-verbal ones like a shift in posture, a sound, or a change in play.

Try responding to any communication attempt — a point, a sound, a word approximation — as a real message. This builds your child's confidence that communicating (in any form) gets a response, which encourages more of it over time.

modules.name: Child-Raising Behavior and Management Guide
modules.description: Practical, day-to-day strategies for routines, transitions, and calm responses to big emotions.

articles.title: Creating Predictable Routines
articles.html:
Structured, predictable routines help many children with ASD feel safe and reduce daily friction. Predictability lowers the number of unknowns a child has to process, which frees up energy for learning and connection.

  • Keep wake-up, meals, and bedtime on a consistent rhythm where possible.
  • Give advance warning before transitions ("five more minutes, then bath time").
  • When routines must change, prepare your child ahead of time rather than surprising them.

articles.title: Responding to Meltdowns with Calm
articles.html:
A meltdown is not a tantrum aimed at getting something — it's often a nervous system in overload. The most effective first response is usually to lower stimulation, not to add more instructions or discipline in the moment.

Try: lowering your voice, reducing eye contact if that helps your child, giving space, and waiting for the wave to pass before talking things through. Afterward, a brief, calm conversation about what happened (once your child is regulated) helps more than an in-the-moment lecture.

If meltdowns involve risk of harm to your child or others, consult your child's therapist or pediatrician for an individualized safety plan.

articles.title: Positive Reinforcement Basics
articles.html:
Noticing and rewarding the behavior you want to see — specifically and immediately — tends to be more effective than only correcting the behavior you don't want.

Be specific: "I love how you used your words to ask for a break" works better than a generic "good job." Small, consistent, genuine praise builds motivation over time far more reliably than occasional big rewards.

modules.name: Learning and School Support Section
modules.description: Home-school collaboration, understanding IEPs, and reducing homework stress.

articles.title: Working With Your Child's School
articles.html:
Strong home-school collaboration helps strategies stay consistent across both settings — which matters a lot for children who thrive on predictability.

  • Share what works at home (calming strategies, communication tools) with teachers directly.
  • Ask for regular short check-ins rather than waiting for a crisis to communicate.
  • Keep a simple shared notebook or messaging thread between home and the classroom.

articles.title: Individualized Education Plans, Explained
articles.html:
An Individualized Education Plan (or a SPED learning plan) outlines specific goals, accommodations, and support tailored to your child's learning profile. It's a living document — one that should be revisited and adjusted as your child grows.

You are a core member of this planning team, not just a signatory. Bring your observations from home; they're often the most detailed data anyone has on your child.

articles.title: Homework Strategies That Reduce Stress
articles.html:
Breaking homework into short, clearly bounded chunks — with visible start and end points — tends to work better than one long unstructured session.

A consistent homework spot, a visual timer, and a small predictable break routine in between tasks can turn homework from a daily battle into a manageable, structured part of the day.

faqs.q: Is C.R.I.B.S. a substitute for therapy or diagnosis?
faqs.a: No. C.R.I.B.S. is a guidance and information tool, not a medical or therapeutic service. It does not diagnose, treat, or replace advice from a licensed developmental pediatrician, therapist, or special education professional.

faqs.q: My child was just diagnosed. Where do I even start?
faqs.a: Start with the Autism Information Module for the basics, then the Professional Support Directory to find a developmental pediatrician or SPED specialist near you. Many parents also find the parent community a helpful place to feel less alone in the first weeks.

faqs.q: How was the content in this app put together?
faqs.a: Content is compiled from published clinical and educational literature on ASD, then reviewed by developmental pediatric specialists, SPED educators, and IT professionals before being simplified for everyday use.

faqs.q: Is C.R.I.B.S. only for use in Taguig City?
faqs.a: The Professional Support Directory currently focuses on Taguig City and nearby areas, since that's where this study was conducted. The guidance content itself is meant to be useful anywhere.

faqs.q: What if a strategy in the app doesn't work for my child?
faqs.a: That's expected — every child on the spectrum is different. Treat each guide as a starting point to adapt, not a strict rulebook. If something consistently isn't working, your child's therapist or SPED educator can help tailor it.

faqs.q: Can I talk to other parents through the app?
faqs.a: Yes — the home screen includes a community feed where you can post a message or question and see posts from other parents and, where noted, from professionals.
